t: Sum of Floored Pairs — Counting Multiples with Prefix Sums
o:
**Understanding the problem**

We must compute the sum of floor(nums[i] / nums[j]) over **all ordered pairs** of indices, including i == j, modulo $10^9 + 7$. With n up to 10^5 there are up to 10^10 pairs, so visiting every pair individually is hopeless.

**Walking through Example 1:** nums = [2,5,9]. Divisions yielding 0: floor(2/5), floor(2/9), floor(5/9). Yielding 1: the three self-divisions plus floor(9/5). Yielding more: floor(5/2) = 2 and floor(9/2) = 4. Total = 0 + 4 + 2 + 4 = 10.

**Example 2:** [7,7,7,7,7,7,7] has 7 * 7 = 49 ordered pairs and every division floors to 1, so the answer is 49 — a hint that duplicates matter and equal values should be handled through frequencies rather than element-by-element.

**What the constraints imply:** both n and nums[i] are bounded by 10^5, which invites bucket counting keyed on values. For a fixed divisor y the quotient floor(x / y) takes only max/y distinct values, so organizing work by divisors and their multiples costs sum(max/y) ~ max * ln(max) ~ 1.2 million block queries — comfortably fast.
k: Ordered pairs include self-pairs: every element contributes floor(x/x) = 1, so the answer is always at least n.
Compress duplicates into a frequency array — only the multiset of values matters, never the indices.
floor(x/y) stays constant across each block [q*y, q*y + y - 1]; a prefix-sum of value counts tells how many elements fall inside a block in O(1).
Enumerating divisors and multiples touches sum(max/y) ~ max * ln(max) ~ 1.2 * 10^6 value pairs despite n = 10^5.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over All Pairs
a.i: Translate the definition literally: loop over every ordered pair of indices and accumulate floor(nums[i]/nums[j]). Trivially correct and a useful baseline for reasoning, but at n = 10^5 this executes about 10^10 divisions — far beyond any time limit.
s: For each index i, for each index j, add floor(nums[i] / nums[j]) to the accumulator.
a.t: O(n^2) — every ordered pair is processed once; roughly 10^10 operations at n = 10^5, so this times out.
a.sp: O(1) — just an accumulator beyond the input.

a.i: Equal values produce equal quotients, so collapse nums into its D distinct values with frequencies. The contribution of dividend value x against divisor value y is freq[x] * freq[y] * floor(x/y), evaluated once rather than once per pair of copies. Example 2 collapses to a single value and finishes instantly — but D can reach 10^5 when values are all distinct, leaving a worst case near 10^10 operations.
s: Build a frequency map of nums and collect its distinct keys.
For every ordered pair of distinct values (x, y), add freq[x] * freq[y] * floor(x / y).
Reduce modulo 10^9 + 7 during accumulation and return.
a.t: O(n + D^2) — building frequencies is linear, then all pairs of D distinct values are examined; D can be 10^5, so the worst case is quadratic in D.
a.sp: O(D) — the frequency map holds at most D entries.

a.i: Fix the divisor value y. As the dividend x grows, floor(x/y) equals q exactly for x in the block [q*y, q*y + y - 1]. With prefix counts pref (pref[v] = number of elements <= v), each block contributes q times the count of elements inside it, answered in O(1). Sweeping all blocks for every present y costs sum over y of max/y ~ max ln max ~ 1.2 million additions. Multiplying each subtotal by cnt[y] accounts for every copy of y acting as the denominator.
s: Bucket-count occurrences into cnt and build pref where pref[v] counts elements <= v.
For each y with cnt[y] > 0, walk blocks starting at lo = y, 2y, 3y, ... while lo <= max.
For each block add q * (pref[min(max, lo + y - 1)] - pref[lo - 1]) to a running total, where q = lo / y.
Add cnt[y] * total to the global answer modulo 10^9 + 7.
a.t: O(n + max log max) — bucketing is linear and the divisor/multiple sweep performs sum(max/d) ~ max ln max ~ 1.2 * 10^6 additions for max = 10^5.
a.sp: O(max) — two integer arrays of size max + 1 dominate memory.

w: Sketch the brute force briefly, then pivot to value-space reasoning: deduplication (Approach 2) sells the frequency insight, and the harmonic sweep (Approach 3) is what you should land on in an interview. Pitfalls: forgetting ordered pairs means both (i, j) and (j, i) count, plus every i == j self-pair adds 1; applying the modulus too late lets intermediate products overflow 64-bit types in C++/Java, so reduce per step; off-by-one errors at block boundaries are avoided by consistently computing the range count as pref[hi] - pref[lo - 1]. Edge cases worth stating: a single-element array answers 1, and arrays full of one value answer n * n. Likely follow-ups: the same block-enumeration skeleton solves tasks like counting pairs with x divisible by y or gcd-convolution style sums; if values reached 10^9, neither bucketing nor harmonic enumeration applies and you would need sorting plus per-element binary searches instead.
